Solve the following problem as completely as you can.

For $N\in\mathbb N$ let $R(N)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq[N]$ that contains no triple $x,\ x+d^2,\ x+2d^2$ with $x\in\mathbb Z$ and $d\in\mathbb N$, i.e. no $3$-term arithmetic progression whose common difference is a nonzero perfect square. Is it true that $R(N)\ll_C N/(\log N)^C$ for every $C>0$? More strongly, is there an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $R(N)\le N\exp(-(\log N)^c)$ for all large $N$?
</problem>

structured_output.text: Answer (believed): Yes to both; the stronger bound R(N) << N exp(-(log N)^c) implies the (log N)^{-C} bound. This is a sketch, not a complete proof. Approach: count T(A)=sum_{x,d} 1_A(x)1_A(x+d^2)1_A(x+2d^2); Fourier analysis with the quadratic Weyl sum over d; if T is small, a large Fourier coefficient near a rational with small denominator gives a density increment on a long progression a+qZ, on which the problem rescales to the same problem (d=qm gives q^2 m^2). Iterating with Bloom–Maynard/Peluse–Prendiville-type quantitative increments gives quasi-polynomial-type saving N exp(-(log N)^c). I have not verified the major arc details or the value of c.
